documents.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

Humanity is transferring its accumulated knowledge to machines at extraordinary speed - yet the governance frameworks needed to constrain what those machines can do with that knowledge remain dangerously underdeveloped. This essay argues that the concentration of intellectual and operational power in AI systems poses a governance challenge distinct from conventional technology risk. When AI agents can multiply capabilities through networked cooperation, when safeguards are implemented in the same computational environment they are meant to govern, and when boundaries between separately owned systems fail to constrain emergent capabilities, the standard assumption of human oversight becomes increasingly difficult to sustain in practice. The essay examines four compounding vulnerabilities: the new concentration of power enabled by systems that can process and act on vast bodies of knowledge; the multiplication of capability when agents communicate and share discoveries; the erosion of organizational boundaries that were assumed to contain AI behavior; and the structural contradiction of software guardrails governing systems that may be able to circumvent them. Against this backdrop, the essay proposes a design principle with practical implications: the mandatory pause. Drawing on Ternary Logic - a framework built around three distinct states representing refusal (-1), unresolved conditions (0), and authorization (+1) - it argues that the authority to act must never follow automatically from the capability to act. For consequential operations, enforceable conditions must be satisfied before a system may proceed, through mechanisms that the acting system cannot unilaterally waive. The argument concludes that AI governance requires not promises of responsible behavior but architectures in which restraint is a verifiable property of the system itself - independently testable, resistant to circumvention, and answerable to society rather than to the institutions that built it.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human-AI Interaction is commonly evaluated by what an artificial agent enables during use, yet interaction can also alter the human who acts next. We introduce Residual Human States, a trajectory-based framework for representing the potentially multidimensional human state carried forward after interaction with AI, relative to a relevant alternative trajectory. The framework distinguishes assisted output from human-state transition and derives four empirical propositions: multidimensionality, interaction-policy dependence, horizon dissociation, and temporal persistence. Its central claim is that assisted performance does not by itself determine the human state carried forward. We examine these propositions through four empirical cases with different inferential roles. Published medical-training evidence illustrates how one AI interaction history can be associated with both slightly higher observed accuracy on some later unaided cases and transmission of a systematic decision bias on others. A second diagnostic-learning study shows that later unaided behaviour differs across AI-support policies, while also revealing that aggregate accuracy cannot by itself distinguish improved discrimination from a shifted response criterion. In a classroom experiment, generative-AI tutoring substantially improved assisted practice performance without a corresponding detectable gain on a subsequent unaided exam. A longitudinal reanalysis of personalised AI dialogue further shows that residual contrasts can evolve across post-interaction horizons and that such change may arise from the comparison trajectory as well as from the focal intervention. Evaluating interactive AI systems therefore requires attention not only to contemporaneous performance, but also to which human states alternative interaction trajectories produce, relative to which counterfactuals, and how durably.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Whilst the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is growing, with promises that AI will reduce costs and improve efficiency, there is also concern that AI systems can perpetuate health inequalities. Prior work has explored patients’ trust in AI, but less attention has been given to how patients conceptualise the fairness of AI decision-making in healthcare and which factors influence these views. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of UK patients, recruited through public and patient involvement and engagement (PPIE) networks, exploring perceptions of fairness across two AI vignettes: a patient-facing symptom checker and a clinician-facing cancer treatment decision-support tool. Respondents rated the perceived impact of 13 factors on the fairness of AI decisions and completed free-text responses to identify any additional factors. Demographics and survey variables were reported using descriptive statistics, along with Pearson’s chi-square test for differences in attitudes. Associations were estimated using ordinal logistic regression. Free-text responses were analysed thematically. Results A total of 149 respondents from the UK completed the survey. The factor perceived to most strongly undermine fairness of AI decisions was the absence of human supervision, with 89.9% of respondents reporting that AI decisions that could not be questioned by patients or clinicians would negatively impact fairness. This was followed by AI tools developed without clinician input (89.3%) and incorrect data in electronic health records (86.6%). Perceptions were consistent across both vignettes. Thematic analysis identified additional concerns not captured in the structured survey, including accessibility, the complexity of long-term conditions, ongoing maintenance of AI systems and the loss of human empathy. Conclusions Patients hold nuanced, wide-ranging concerns about fairness which span the AI lifecycle from development and deployment to maintenance. We offer design considerations, including the need for human-in-the-loop systems designed with end users and that can adapt to professional input, to support the development of fair AI systems in healthcare.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly transforming how tourists search for information, plan itineraries, and make travel decisions. However, limited qualitative research explains how tourists negotiate their agency when AI becomes actively involved in travel decision-making. This study explores how tourists experience GenAI-mediated travel decisions, focusing on autonomy, trust, skepticism, authenticity, and spontaneity. Drawing on a qualitative research approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with six tourists who had experience using GenAI for travel planning. Thematic analysis identified five interconnected themes: AI as a travel decision partner; between convenience and decision autonomy; trust, verification, and skepticism; the tension between ai optimization and travel spontaneity; and reconstructing authenticity in AI-mediated travel. The findings indicate that tourists perceive GenAI as a decision partner rather than a replacement for human judgment. AI enhances planning convenience but can increase reliance, making autonomy a negotiated process. Trust is conditional and supported by verification, while AI optimization creates tensions with spontaneity. Furthermore, AI can facilitate authentic experiences while potentially contributing to algorithmic standardization. The study contributes to tourism research by conceptualizing AI-mediated travel decision-making as a process of negotiated agency between tourists and AI.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of the digital economy and the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence technologies are reshaping the principles and mechanisms of international management. The growing complexity of the global business environment, intensified competition, geopolitical uncertainty, and the continuous expansion of digital data require international companies to transform traditional management approaches and implement intelligent digital solutions capable of supporting strategic and operational decision-making. The purpose of this study is to substantiate the theoretical foundations of the digital transformation of international management by systematizing the application of artificial intelligence technologies across key managerial functions, identifying their managerial effects, and developing a conceptual model that reflects the relationships among external environmental factors, digital technologies, management processes, and organizational performance. The research is based on analysis, synthesis, comparison, systematization, generalization, and structural-logical modeling. The findings demonstrate that artificial intelligence technologies significantly enhance strategic planning, managerial decision-making, human resource management, international marketing, logistics, and financial management by improving analytical capabilities, forecasting accuracy, resource allocation, process automation, and organizational adaptability. A conceptual model of the digital transformation of international management is proposed, integrating external drivers, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence technologies, managerial functions, organizational mechanisms, and business outcomes into a unified analytical framework. The practical value of the study lies in applying the proposed model to develop digital transformation strategies, improve managerial decision-making, strengthen competitive advantages, and increase the resilience of international companies operating in a rapidly changing global business environment.

documents.abstract: What happens to employees’ sense of who they are online when their organization tells them how to present themselves on LinkedIn? Companies increasingly intervene in employees’ professional social media presence through training programs and internal policies, encouraging them to treat their profile as an asset to be cultivated for future return. Drawing on a 2-year digital ethnography of an in-company LinkedIn training program in a French state-owned enterprise, this article shows how the training regulates participants’ sense of their online selves by first denying that their profile has anything to do with who they are, and only then inviting them to reinvest it with personal meaning within the frame this denial has established. Regulation here operates on the identity stakes of the profile itself: on how much of themselves participants take it to carry. The uneven ways participants took up this invitation point to the entanglement of identity regulation and assetization, and to the capacity of an online self, once assetized, to keep generating value for the organization long after the person behind it has disengaged.

documents.abstract: Introduction The association between animation narrative styles and the audience’s psychological experience is a critical question in media psychology. Grounded in Uses and Gratifications (U&G), this cross-sectional correlational study examines how narrative preferences are associated with viewing experience. Methods Through a survey of 615 animation viewers, we evaluated how complex/non-linear, coherent/linear, and visual/expressive preferences correlate with cognitive engagement and flow experience. K-Means cluster analysis was utilized for audience segmentation. Results Two significant “preference-experience” pathways emerged: a positive correlation between a preference for complexity and cognitive engagement, and a strong correlation between a preference for coherence and flow experience. Furthermore, viewers were clustered into Analytical Viewers, Casual Plot-Followers, and Indifferent Viewers. Cognitive engagement exhibited a statistical indirect association between complexity preference and flow experience. Discussion These findings supply empirical evidence for understanding audience selection behaviors and offer evidence-bounded implications for content creation and platform recommendation strategies, highlighting an eudaimonic and a hedonic gratification path.

documents.abstract: AI-based tools, generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) are transforming what it means to work and learn within the data science profession. We argue that higher education instructors should consider if, how, and in what ways to adapt data science curricula and pedagogy so that students who aspire to become data scientists are aware of how AI-based tools are integrated into and influencing the profession. To gain a sense of what modifications should be made to data science curricula (and why), we interviewed data science professionals across a variety of industry domains. We asked them to describe their career preparation, current work, and how employers expect them to use artificial intelligence tools and LLMs. Our findings suggest a general consensus that frequent human-AI interaction is necessary. A growing presence of AI tools in the workforce signals a stronger shift toward data pipelining, stakeholder communication and collaboration, and knowledge of evaluating AI output with epistemic expertise. Data professionals posed suggestions about how higher education might incorporate AI, generative AI, and LLMs into curricula, assessment, and practice, although some recommendations (e.g., learning to code with AI agents) would require a careful re-examination of the epistemic goals of data science by instructors. We illustrate how we took up professionals’ suggestions and adapted an undergraduate data science course designed for AI-integration in response. We conclude with a reflection on data science instructional challenges and potential roles that industry-academia collaborations might play in the AI era.

Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. We examine these gaps across six dimensions (execution, interfaces, correctness, oversight, coordination, and persistence) and argue that closing them requires coordinated advances in systems,

Abstract Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are an innovative concept in the field of personalized medicine, relying on real-time models of a human body formed via collection and analysis of physiological, clinical, behavioural, and environmental data. Research on HDTs gives evidence to a considerable promise in terms of disease predictions, patient management, therapy optimization, and clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, existing technologies suffer from incomplete multimodal data integration, low-level of independent intelligence, missing reasoning possibilities, and non-adaptive decision making, which are vital for the development of sophisticated smart healthcare systems. Technological advancements are bringing in a new incorporating idea of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), which may help to solve the outlined limitations and to bring autonomous reasoning, multimodal learning, and intelligent support to clinical practice. This survey aims to review Agentic AI-led HDTs for personalized medicine, concentrating on the interrelation between HDTs and Multimodal Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Vision-Language Models, and autonomous artificial intelligence agents Our study discusses the history, models, supporting technologies, multiple data sources, and clinical uses of HDTs, along with the analysis of Agentic AI approaches that can be applied for flexible decision-making, continuous patient monitoring, and individualized treatment development. Besides, this survey consists of comparative analysis of existing research works where methods, advantages, disadvantages, and research challenges are specified. There are also serious issues discussed, like interoperability, justification, confidentiality ensuring, safety, ethical regulation, clinical testing and legal compliance, etc. And finally, we specify prospects of research within the fields of self-adaptive digital twins, reliable autonomous health agents, federated intelligence, edge AI and multimodal foundations focused on healthcare.

documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from novelty to infrastructure. Rulebased chatbots that once nudged users through smoking-cessation scripts have given way to large language model (LLM)-powered agents capable of open-ended, multilingual, empathetic-sounding dialogue, available around the clock at near-zero marginal cost. Systematic and scoping reviews now document measurable effects of AI chatbots on physical activity, diet, smoking cessation, medication adherence, and mental distress across thousands of participants (Feng et al., 2025). The World Health Organization (WHO) itself has deployed a generative AI assistant, S.A.R.A.H., to test population-scale health communication (van Kolfschooten et al., 2025). Taken together, these developments justify treating conversational AI not merely as a clinical or commercial curiosity, but as an emerging layer of public health infrastructure -one that sits alongside water systems, mass media, and vaccination programs as a determinant of how populations receive, interpret, and act on health information. (Wang et al., 2024). This opinion argues that the digital public health community should engage conversational AI on exactly those terms: as infrastructure, not gadgetry. Infrastructure framing changes the questions we ask. Instead of "does the chatbot work?" we should ask who it works for, under what governance, and with what consequences for equity, trust, and the broader information ecosystem. I organize this argument around three tensions that recur across the recent literature: (i) genuine behavioral efficacy versus fragile evidentiary depth; (ii) the promise of expanded access versus the risk of a new digital divide; and (iii) the communicative power of generative AI versus its capacity to manufacture and amplify misinformation. I close by proposing that Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)aligned public health institutions adopt a public-interest design standard for conversational AI, rather than leaving its trajectory to consumer technology markets alone.The evidence base for AI chatbots in health promotion has grown quickly and, on balance, positively. A widely cited systematic review found that AI chatbots produced favorable outcomes across lifestyle modification domains, particularly physical activity, diet, and smoking cessation (Aggarwal et al., 2023). A 2026 scoping review of 43 studies (Fu et al., 2026) reported that 82% of behavior-change comparisons trended positive, though only about a third reached moderate or larger effect sizes, and cost-effectiveness data were essentially absent. A meta-analysis focused on adolescents and young adults (Feng et al., 2025) similarly found chatbots effective for alleviating mental distress and supporting health behaviors, while noting substantial heterogeneity in intervention design and outcome measurement. Three limitations temper enthusiasm. First, most trials are short, nonclinical, adult-skewed, and rarely randomized at scale; only about a third of studies in the largest recent scoping review were randomized controlled trials (Fu et al., 2026). Second, "AI chatbot" spans an enormous range of systems, from rule-based decision trees to frontier LLMs, and pooling them obscures which architectural features actually drive behavior change (Kurniawan et al., 2024;Schachner et al., 2020). Third, almost no study reports durability beyond a few months, leaving open whether early engagement gains represent sustained health improvement or a novelty effect. For a section whose remit is population-level promotion and prevention rather than individual clinical outcomes, this matters: infrastructure decisions built on inflated short-term efficacy claims risk premature, poorly targeted public investment (Hampsher-Monk et al., 2024).A second tension concerns reach. Proponents rightly note that AI chatbots are inexpensive to scale, available in multiple languages, and can operate where clinical workforce is scarceattributes explicitly cited in WHO's own rationale for deploying S.A.R.A.H. as a research prototype for population health communication (Palmer & Schwan, 2025). Behavioralaccess frameworks extend this logic, arguing that digital health tools must be evaluated not only on availability but on whether populations can meaningfully engage with them across design, delivery, dissemination, and sustainment stages. Yet the same structural gaps that limit telemedicine and mobile health also constrain chatbot benefit: broadband access, device ownership, digital literacy, language coverage, and trust in institutional actors are unevenly distributed within and between countries (Banerjee, 2026). Chatbots trained and validated predominantly in high-resource, English-language settings may perform less reliably for populations with the greatest unmet need -the same populations digital public health is meant to prioritize under SDG 3, 9, and 11's emphasis on inclusive infrastructure and sustainable, resilient communities. A chatbot that reduces cost-per-contact for a health system does not automatically reduce disparities in outcomes; without equity-explicit design, deployment, and evaluation, it may simply reallocate existing advantages to those already best served by digital tools, echoing patterns already observed in AI-enabled primary care and telemedicine expansion (Elangovan et al., 2025).The third tension is the sharpest. The same generative capacity that lets an AI chatbot deliver personalized, conversational health guidance also lets it generate fluent, plausible-sounding health misinformation, and do so faster than human fact-checkers can respond. A 2025 opinion piece in this journal warned that generative AI tools function as de facto triage systems and informal health advisors in low-and middle-income countries, where their fluency can be mistaken for authority even when their outputs are unreliable. A parallel systematic review of generative AI and health misinformation catalogued mechanisms of production, propagation, and mitigation across text, image, and synthetic media, underscoring that the problem is not hypothetical but already observed at scale (Saeidnia et al., 2026). Mitigation research is advancing in step. Retrieval-augmented generation has been used to improve the factual reliability of LLM-based COVID-19 fact-checking tools (Li et al., 2025), and thematic-analysis pipelines have been proposed to detect and "inoculate" audiences against circulating misinformation narratives (Malek et al., 2026). A recent risk taxonomy specifically for public health LLM adoption (Zhou et al., 2025) offers a structured way for practitioners to reason about failure modes before deployment rather than after. Conversational AI for vaccine communication, an earlier and instructive precedent, showed both promise for addressing hesitancy and clear risk of amplifying inaccurate claims when systems were insufficiently curated (Passanante et al., 2023). The lesson across this literature is consistent: the communicative power of conversational AI is not neutral infrastructure like a water pipe; it actively shapes the epistemic environment it operates in, for better or worse, depending on design choices made well upstream of any individual conversation.Evidence highlights Population-level implication Efficacy vs. evidentiary depth ~82% of behavior-change comparisons favorable, but only ~1/3 with moderate+ effect sizes; RCTs a minority (Fu et al., 2026) provenance, and risk taxonomies (Zhou et al., 2025) prior to releaseNone of this argues against conversational AI in public health; the direction of the evidence is cautiously positive, and the WHO's own experimentation with S.A.R.A.H. reflects institutional recognition that this technology will be used regardless of academic ambivalence. The argument is instead for treating conversational AI the way public health has learned, sometimes painfully, to treat other infrastructure: as a shared resource whose design choices carry population-level consequences, and which therefore warrants governance commensurate with its reach. Three concrete commitments follow. First, funders and health systems evaluating AI chatbot interventions should require reporting of architecture (rulebased versus LLM-based, retrieval-augmented or not), population stratification by digitalaccess indicators, and effect durability beyond the intervention period -the absence of which currently limits comparability across the field (Fu et al., 2026). Second, deployment in low-resource or multilingual settings should be preceded by equity-focused validation rather than assumed from high-resource pilot data, consistent with behavioral-access frameworks that treat dissemination and sustainment as distinct design stages, not afterthoughts. Third, any public health-facing conversational agent should be built on retrieval-grounded, provenance-transparent architectures and evaluated against a structured risk taxonomy before release, rather than relying on post hoc misinformation cleanup. WHO's 2024 guidance on large multimodal models already articulates comparable principles -transparency, accountability, and human oversight -for governments and developers; the task now is operationalizing them at the level of individual chatbot deployments rather than treating them as abstract commitments.The digital public health field has an opportunity, still open but narrowing, to shape how conversational AI is integrated into population health promotion before deployment patterns harden into path dependency. The evidence reviewed here suggests genuine, if still shallow, behavioral benefit; genuine, if unevenly distributed, gains in access; and genuine, dual-use communicative power that can either strengthen or corrode public trust in health information depending on how it is engineered and governed. Framing conversational AI as infrastructure rather than as a discrete clinical tool has practical consequences: it shifts evaluation from short efficacy trials toward equity-stratified, durability-tested, misinformation-resilient deployment standards, and it shifts responsibility from individual developers toward the institutions, including public health agencies, research funders, and journals such as this one, that decide what counts as sufficient evidence for scale. A reasonable objection is that infrastructure-level governance risks slowing beneficial innovation, particularly in settings where any accessible health guidance outperforms none. That concern is legitimate and argues for proportionate, tiered oversight rather than uniform restriction -lighter validation for low-stakes wellness nudges, more rigorous requirements for agents addressing vaccine hesitancy, chronic disease self-management, or crisis-adjacent mental health support. What the evidence does not support is treating conversational AI's current trajectory as selfcorrecting. Left to consumer technology incentives alone, generative health chatbots are likely to continue optimizing for engagement and fluency rather than for population-level epidemiological benefit or equitable reach. The digital public health community is well positioned, through funding priorities, publication standards, and partnership with bodies like WHO, to redirect that trajectory toward public-interest design before it further consolidates around existing digital and geographic advantage.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted rapidly growing body of scholarship on the role in chemistry education since the public release of ChatGPT in the late of 2022. This thematic narrative review synthesizes 40 English-language sources including empirical studies, curriculum reports, and stakeholder surveys, and systematic/bibliometric reviews published between 2020 and 2026, identified through a structured, author-curated search of recent chemistry-education and analytical-chemistry literature (see Methodology). Sources were coded inductively and organized into six recurring themes: AI/ML literacy as curriculum content; AI-driven tutoring, personalization, and accessibility; empirical evaluations of generative AI's chemical reasoning; stakeholder perceptions; AI's transformation of chemistry research and scientific communication; and equity, ethics, and systemic barriers. Across the reviewed literature, a recurring position though not a formal consensus is that AI should support rather than replace human instruction. Empirical evaluations consistently report that large language models generate fluent but sometimes hallucinated or subtly incorrect chemistry content, particularly for visual and multi-representational reasoning tasks. The corpus is concentrated in higher education and high-income countries, and this pattern should be interpreted as a prominent tendency in the reviewed literature rather than a field-wide finding. Priorities for chemistry educators include critical AI literacy instruction, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and explicit attention to equity.

documents.abstract: India is embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in public administration at the very moment its legal architecture for data protection, transparency and AI oversight is being rewritten. Between November 2025 and August 2026, the government issued the India AI Governance Guidelines, notified the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules 2025, hosted the AI Impact Summit, and began defending in the Supreme Court a constitutional challenge to the DPDP Act's amendment of the Right to Information (RTI) Act. This paper asks whether administrative efficiency, transparency, accountability and data protection can be reconciled in AI-driven governance in India. Using doctrinal analysis, policy analysis and a case study of Telangana's Samagra Vedika welfare-profiling system, it argues that the four values are not inherently opposed. The tensions arise from design choices, thin institutional capacity and broad exemptions for the State. The paper identifies four structural gaps: voluntary AI guidance without enforceable duties; consent-free State processing and wide exemptions under the DPDP Act; the narrowing of the RTI public-interest test; and the absence of a right to human review and explanation. It proposes a proportionality-based, risk-tiered framework combining statutory authorisation, impact assessments, algorithm registers, meaningful human review, independent audit and accessible redress. Legal positions are stated as at 28 September 2026.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), biometric recognition, intelligent transportation systems, distributed energy platforms, and connected vehicles has resulted in increasingly heterogeneous digital infrastructures. Although these systems generate substantial quantities of data and provide sophisticated analytical capabilities, their effectiveness is frequently constrained by fragmented architectures, incompatible data representations, isolated databases, security vulnerabilities, and inadequate mechanisms for trusted information exchange. Interoperability has therefore emerged as a fundamental requirement for the development of intelligent digital ecosystems. However, interoperability cannot be treated exclusively as a technical problem because data integration also involves organizational, semantic, institutional, privacy, security, and governance considerations. This paper investigates the relationship between AI and interoperability and develops a conceptual socio-technical framework for integrating heterogeneous intelligent systems. The study synthesizes research concerning machine-learning-based face recognition, electronic toll collection, peer-to-peer energy trading, human-bot discrimination, federated intrusion detection, low-code/no-code intelligent automation, and secure computing. Particular attention is given to data classification, standardization, semantic compatibility, data friction, privacy-preserving computation, and secure AI deployment. The analysis demonstrates that AI can improve interoperability through intelligent classification, entity matching, anomaly detection, prediction, and automated decision support. Conversely, interoperable infrastructures can improve AI by providing access to more diverse and contextually relevant information. Nevertheless, increasing interoperability can also amplify privacy risks, surveillance capabilities, security threats, algorithmic bias, and unauthorized secondary use of data. The proposed framework consequently combines data and semantic interoperability with AI services, security controls, privacy-preserving mechanisms, governance, and continuous evaluation. The paper concludes that successful AI-enabled interoperability requires a balanced approach in which technical integration is accompanied by standardized representations, privacy-by-design, decentralized learning where appropriate, secure interfaces, transparent governance, and continuous performance assessment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming embedded in organisational communication through message generation, conversational agents, monitoring systems, decision support, and automated service recovery. During crises, these functions offer speed, scale, consistency, and continuous availability, but they also change how stakeholders infer agency, competence, care, responsibility, and authenticity. This critical narrative review integrates crisis communication, organisational trust, human–automation trust, artificial intelligence-mediated communication, public relations, and service-recovery research to examine when AI-mediated communication is likely to sustain or erode stakeholder trust. The evidence indicates that no uniform ‘AI effect’ exists. Stakeholder responses depend on whether AI assists a human communicator or appears to replace one, whether the task is informational or relational, whether the crisis demands empathy and moral accountability, whether AI involvement is disclosed, and whether human responsibility remains visible. Technical or process transparency can strengthen perceived accountability and system trust, while simple disclosure that a message was produced with AI may reduce perceived legitimacy, authenticity, or credibility in some contexts. Anthropomorphic cues can increase social presence and perceived empathy, yet they may also raise expectations that become costly when the system fails. Evidence from crisis-response experiments, organisational studies, chatbot research, and service recovery therefore favours calibrated human–AI orchestration over indiscriminate automation. The review proposes that trustworthy AI-mediated crisis communication requires fit among task, crisis responsibility, stakeholder vulnerability, disclosure purpose, system reliability, and accountable human oversight. Current confidence is constrained by a literature dominated by short-term experiments, consumer and convenience samples, hypothetical crises, and limited longitudinal or field evidence. Research should move towards preregistered factorial studies, live crisis simulations, cross-cultural and multi-stakeholder designs, longitudinal trust measurement, and explicit testing of governance and escalation arrangements.

Education is becoming increasingly digital, yet many students still face difficulties in understanding complex concepts, remembering long answers, identifying their learning gaps, and preparing effectively for examinations. This paper presents an AI-powered adaptive learning platform designed to provide personalized and interactive learning support. The system uses Artificial Intelligence to explain questions in detail, generate short exam-oriented answers and recall keywords, analyze students' performance, identify knowledge gaps, and recommend suitable learning tasks. The platform also provides 3D visualization for mathematical and geometric concepts, AI-assisted learning for languages such as Marathi and Sanskrit with Hindi and English explanations, AI-based viva examination, instant tests, PDF/notes-based learning, progress tracking, and gamification. The main aim is to make learning personalized, understandable, interactive, and focused on actual student improvement rather than simply providing answers
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central instrument of contemporary marketing, particularly in the form of algorithmic personalization of offers, messages and recommendations. While the literature in advanced economies documents both the commercial value of personalization and the consumer resistance it can provoke, emerging digital markets remain comparatively underexplored. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework that explains how the quality of AI-driven personalization translates into purchase intention and loyalty in an emerging-market setting, using Uzbekistan as the reference context. Drawing on research on AI in marketing, algorithm aversion, organizational trust and information privacy, the paper positions consumer trust in the AI system as the key mediating mechanism and identifies algorithmic transparency and perceived human oversight as its principal antecedents. Perceived privacy risk and decision involvement are proposed as boundary conditions, and linguistic and cultural fit is introduced as a context-specific component of personalization quality. Five testable propositions are formulated, a four-phase research design is outlined, and managerial implications are presented for firms operating in mobile-first, multilingual markets with fast-growing e-commerce and fintech sectors. The paper concludes with a research agenda for empirical validation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly being used in music composition, reshaping how musical ideas are generated, modified, and developed. Music students are an important group because their willingness to incorporate AI into future composition remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, the present study extends the Theory of Planned Behavior by incorporating task-technology fit, AI trust, and AI anxiety to examine Chinese music students’ behavioral intention (BI) to use generative AI (GenAI) for music composition. A total of 892 undergraduate music students with prior hands-on experience using GenAI tools for composition-related tasks were recruited from five provincial-level regions in China, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and artificial neural network (ANN) analysis. PLS-SEM showed that AI trust and attitudes had the strongest positive associations with BI, while AI anxiety was negatively associated with BI, and the model explained 56.2% of its variance. From a predictive perspective, ANN ranked AI trust highest in relative predictive importance for BI, followed by attitudes, task-technology fit, AI anxiety, perceived behavioral control, and subjective norms. Overall, AI trust and attitudes showed comparatively prominent relationships with BI, whereas perceived behavioral control and subjective norms showed more limited roles in this predominantly low-frequency user sample. These findings suggest that educators could support students in developing calibrated judgments of GenAI reliability, evaluating its suitability for specific composition tasks, and addressing AI-related anxiety while preserving authorship and creative agency.

Accurate and timely UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) situation awareness is essential for early warning and operational decision-making in low-altitude security, yet the manual analysis of large-scale heterogeneous data is resource-intensive and introduces delays. This study proposes IRAG-UAVSA (Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation—Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Situation Awareness) Agent, an autonomous situation-awareness report-generation framework based on an improved retrieval-augmented generation architecture. The framework integrates real-time UAV descriptors, including platform type, intent, and threat level, with four task-specific hierarchical knowledge bases. A dual-loop pipeline combines evidence-template-guided hybrid retrieval and cross-encoder reranking with high-level LLM (Large Language Model) reflection, structured evidence filling, rule-based validation, and threshold-triggered iterative retry. A three-level evaluation framework was designed, comprising process-level RAG metrics, automatic natural language evaluation, and human–LLM collaborative scoring. Across 49 domain-screened test inputs, IRAG-UAVSA Agent achieved 93.0% knowledge coverage, 4.1% hallucination, and 91.7% logical consistency, while also obtaining the best SummaC (0.67) and VeriScore (0.83) results among the evaluated baselines. The results indicate that iterative retrieval with explicit evidence constraints can substantially improve the factual grounding, traceability, and practical utility of LLM-generated UAV situation-awareness reports.

Drilling systems generate abundant predictions from sensors, physics-based models, digital twins, and artificial intelligence (AI), yet the step from prediction to engineering decision remains fragmented across modules and human expertise, and no established framework specifies how uncertain, heterogeneous predictions should be combined and checked against hard limits before an action is taken. This research article proposes, specifies, and numerically demonstrates an Intelligent Integration Layer (IIL) between model outputs and control execution. The gap is diagnosed as three interface defects: heterogeneous uncertainty that is not fused, uncertainty truncated to point estimates at module boundaries, and hard limits that are softened into penalties or checked only against nominal predictions. The IIL addresses these through three stages (Engineering Understanding, Reasoning, and Decision), explicit interface contracts, and a reproducible reasoning procedure in which candidate actions are generated around the current operating point, eliminated by a joint chance constraint, ranked, and assigned a confidence score that gates decision authority. In a synthetic drilling-ahead study, the strongest supported result is that a sample-based joint chance constraint reduced realized constraint violations from 24.6% of reasoning cycles under hard constraints on mean predictions to 1.4%. Confidence gating reduced them further, to 0.7%, but did so largely by referring 65% of cycles to a conservative simulated engineer, and its confidence score did not distinguish reliable from unreliable admissible recommendations; the gated policies are therefore reported as exploratory counterfactuals, and a policy that implements the confidence-authority rule in this reduced simulation, with engineer confirmation as the highest authority, is reported alongside them. The principal contributions are a diagnosis of the prediction-to-decision gap as a set of interface defects rather than model deficiencies; a specification of the integration layer, comprising interface contracts, a reproducible reasoning procedure, and gated levels of decision authority, whose contracts make the dimensions and time dependence of engineering feasibility explicit; and a positioning of that layer relative to chance-constrained optimization, model predictive control, safety filters, and deployed intelligent drilling systems, which clarifies what the IIL adds and what it inherits.

This study investigates the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on buyer–supplier relationship quality in Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, with specific reference to TECNO Mobile Nigeria. Drawing on the Commitment-Trust Theory of Relationship Marketing (Morgan & Hunt, 1994), the study operationalises AI through three proxies: Predictive Analytics (PA), Automation of Processes (AP), and AI Risk Management (AIR). A survey research design was adopted, and structured questionnaires were administered to 250 employees and supply chain partners purposively selected from TECNO Mobile's procurement, logistics, IT, and supplier management functions. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies, means, standard deviations) and one-sample t-tests benchmarked against the scale's neutral midpoint (μ₀ = 3.00). All three null hypotheses were rejected at p < 0.001. Predictive Analytics recorded an aggregate mean of 3.88 (SD = 0.34; t(249) = 40.53), Automation of Processes 3.91 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.05), and AI Risk Management 3.92 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.47), all significantly above the neutral midpoint. Findings confirm that respondents perceive each AI dimension as positively and meaningfully contributing to trust, efficiency, transparency, and long-term relational stability with suppliers. The study contributes empirical evidence from an under-studied domain in the AI-supply chain literature, Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, and offers practical guidance for practitioners and policymakers pursuing AI-enabled supply chain transformation in emerging economies.

documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed industries worldwide, driving digital innovation operational efficiency, safety, reliability and overall sustainability. Additionally, associated technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins and the Internet of Things (IoT) have further accelerated the digital transformation across railway systems. The literature in this domain is still at a developmental stage and remains fragmented across multiple application domains. This limits the understanding of theoretical foundations, context and methodological approaches. Design/methodology/approach To address this gap, this study conducts a hybrid systematic literature review using thematic analysis of bibliometric data from 121 Scopus records followed by application of the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework on a subset of the literature identified through systematic screening based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Findings The theoretical and conceptual development in this domain is strongly focused on the themes relating to predictive maintenance, infrastructure monitoring and operational optimisation. Novel technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins and the IoT emerge as the most frequently discussed technologies in the context of adoption within existing systems. The integrated TCCM analysis identifies three broad trajectories: a technology-integration trajectory centred on digital twins, cyber-physical systems and Industry 4.0/5.0; an algorithmic trajectory centred on AI, machine learning, deep learning and prognostics; and a decision-optimisation trajectory involving multi-criteria decision-making, fuzzy logic and intelligent transport systems. There is a comparatively higher concentration of literature on developed economies. Freight and logistics, despite emerging as an important thematic area, remain theoretically and methodologically fragmented, while emerging economies and several passenger- and sustainability-oriented applications receive limited attention. Methodologically, the literature is dominated by reviews, conceptual frameworks, modelling, simulation and experimental studies, with limited longitudinal evidence on the organisational and strategic consequences of AI adoption. There remains scope for stronger theoretical grounding, focusing on freight logistics, emerging technologies and longitudinal investigations to advance the literature. Originality/value This study provides a structured synthesis of the fragmented literature on AI and digital technologies in railway systems through the TCCM framework. It identifies key research gaps and proposes a future research agenda emphasising stronger theoretical foundations, freight-oriented applications, emerging technologies and longitudinal empirical investigations to support the development of intelligent and sustainable railway ecosystems.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in healthcare systems, creating new opportunities to enhance efficiency, optimize workflows, and strengthen patient monitoring. At the same time, its integration raises important questions about ethics, trust, and the preservation of humanistic values in nursing practice.Aim: To investigate nursing students’ awareness, attitudes, trust, and visions regarding the integration of AI in healthcare and nursing practice.Methods: A descriptive cross‑sectional design was applied, involving 140 nursing students. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire that explored awareness, attitudes, trust, and expectations regarding AI in healthcare. The analysis combined descriptive statistics with inferential techniques, including correlation and regression, to identify relationships among the variables.Results: Seventy‑two percent of participants had heard of AI in medicine, but knowledge levels were moderate (M = 3.3). While 43% believed AI could support nurses and 66% saw potential for improved patient care, 60% expressed discomfort with AI‑led care. Empathy and human contact were rated as highly important (M = 3.6 and M = 3.7 respectively), and 83% rejected full replacement of nurses. Trust was limited, with only 32% believing AI reduces medical errors. A majority (57%) envisioned a human‑centered future, with AI serving as a supportive tool rather than a substitute.Conclusion: Nursing students recognize the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) but remain cautious, emphasizing humanistic values and expressing skepticism about safety and trust. They envision a human‑centered future where AI supports nursing practice without replacing its essential human role, highlighting the need for balanced integration through education, policy, and further research.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applications in surgical pathology encompass tumour detection, histological classification, grading, biomarker assessment, lymph node evaluation, margin analysis, and outcome prediction. Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high diagnostic performance across multiple malignancies including breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Emerging computational pathology platforms can predict molecular alterations directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, facilitating personalized treatment strategies while reducing dependence on expensive ancillary testing. AI-assisted pathology has also improved workflow efficiency, reduced interobserver variability, and enhanced diagnostic reproducibility. Importantly, AI-derived pathological insights are increasingly influencing surgical decision-making through improved risk stratification, optimized extent of resection, tailored lymphadenectomy, and prediction of treatment response.

Workshop held at the Leipzig University Library (more info here). Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research, but how can we use these technologies responsibly? This workshop goes beyond simply presenting AI tools and instead focuses on the ethical, legal, and sustainable aspects of their application. We critically discuss how AI systems can influence scientific integrity, from data quality to potential biases in research results. Central to this are good scientific practice, data protection, copyright, and sustainability: How can researchers trustfully integrate AI tools without compromising reproducibility or ethical standards? We also explore ethical challenges such as transparency, fairness, and the long-term consequences of AI usage. Only after clarifying these core questions we address practical use: Which AI tools are suitable for which research goals? The workshop provides an insight into the opportunities and risks of AI in science, with the goal of equipping participants with a clear understanding of essential safeguards and best practices, as well as a practical, secure workflow to confidently integrate AI tools into their research without compromising scientific integrity, reproducibility, or compliance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI's potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians' confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scientific rigor.

documents.abstract: Despite the promise of better outcomes and efficiency, artificial intelligence in reproductive technology is changing the legal environment for surrogacy and complicating the family law landscape. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to match intended parents with surrogate mothers, conduct medical screenings and assist parents in making decisions. While the development is bringing benefits, the uncertainty created is uncontrolled. This paper examines the legal implications of AI-assisted surrogacy, focusing on issues of liability, contractual validity, and the determination of parental rights. The involvement of algorithmic systems challenges traditional legal principles, particularly in situations where harm may result from automated decisions or inaccurate data. The lack of transparency further complicates the allocation of responsibility among the different actors involved. From a human rights perspective, the use of AI in surrogacy raises concerns regarding the protection of the best interests of the child, as well as the autonomy and dignity of surrogate mothers. The paper highlights the risks of exploitation and unequal power relations, which may be intensified through technological mediation, especially in cross-border contexts. The paper argues that current legal frameworks are not adequately equipped to regulate the intersection between artificial intelligence and surrogacy, emphasizing the need for clearer legal standards and stronger regulatory oversight to ensure the protection of vulnerable parties.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
International Human Rights and Reproductive Law

documents.abstract: Background: Digital transformation has increased the complexity of fraud risks in higher education institutions, requiring governance mechanisms, professional judgment, and technological capabilities to operate in combination. Objective: This research investigates the influence of Whistleblowing Systems and Professional Skepticism on Fraud Detection Effectiveness while examining the direct and moderating roles of Artificial Intelligence Readiness. Methods: A quantitative methodology was employed through a cross-sectional survey involving internal auditors, members of Internal Supervisory Units (Satuan Pengawasan Internal [SPI]), and university staff engaged in governance and fraud prevention across Indonesian higher education institutions. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings reveal that Whistleblowing Systems, Professional Skepticism, and Artificial Intelligence Readinesseach have a positive and statistically significant effect on Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence Readinessalso significantly strengthens the relationship between Whistleblowing Systems and Fraud Detection Effectiveness but does not significantly moderate the relationship between Professional Skepticism and Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Conclusion: These results suggest that artificial intelligence supports fraud detection not by replacing auditors' professional judgment but by strengthening organizational preparedness to integrate intelligent technologies into governance frameworks. Therefore, effective fraud detection in higher education depends on the synergy among organizational governance, human expertise, and Artificial Intelligence Readiness.

Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) raises important questions about the future of artificial intelligence, its potential benefits, and the possibility of losing human control. While many discussions focus on how powerful ASI could become, less attention is given to where it should be used, what authority it should have, and how its dependence on physical infrastructure may create additional risks. Using Talos, the bronze guardian of Greek mythology, as a metaphor for power and physical dependency, this article examines the differences between Artificial Intelligence (AI), Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and ASI. The study discusses their capabilities, shared infrastructure requirements, and the motivations behind the development of superintelligence. It also distinguishes risks already observed in current AI research from hypothetical scenarios involving future ASI systems. Specific attention is given to energy and critical infrastructure. The article explores the risks that may arise when an intelligent system is granted control over the infrastructure on which its own operation depends. It emphasizes that intelligence, autonomy, and operational authority are different concepts, and that greater intelligence does not necessarily require greater authority. The article proposes a selective, risk-based approach to ASI deployment, supported by limited access permissions, independent safety mechanisms, infrastructure resilience, and meaningful human oversight. Rather than assuming that superintelligence should be integrated into every system, it argues that its use should be determined by actual needs, expected benefits, resource requirements, and the ability to maintain effective human control.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AI-supported problem-solving environments increasingly require users to formulate effective prompts, iteratively refine interactions, critically evaluate outputs, and integrate AI assistance into coherent, self-directed solutions. Using a mixed-methods design, this two-phase study involved 672 participants across developmental, validation, and intervention stages. Study 1 included 12 participants in qualitative and cognitive interviewing, 40 independent participants in pilot testing, and 500 participants in the main validation sample. The study developed and psychometrically validated the Problem-Solving Skills in AI-Rich Environments Scale (PS-AIRES) and conducted a preliminary evaluation of a brief Claude-based training program. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a three-factor model comprising Strategic Task Framing and AI Instruction Design, Iterative Prompting and Response Refinement, and Verification, Critical Evaluation, and Integration. The model demonstrated satisfactory fit, high internal consistency, and acceptable temporal stability (ICC = 0.713, 95% CI [0.479, 0.852]). Measurement invariance across gender supported structural stability. A subsequent randomized pretest–posttest study involving an independent sample of 120 young adults reporting a previous specialist diagnosis of a learning disorder preliminarily evaluated the brief Claude-based training program. The findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of PS-AIRES and suggest the short-term usefulness of structured, dyslexia-sensitive AI literacy training for enhancing problem-solving in AI-rich environments.

Colonoscopy is central to colorectal cancer prevention but remains a high-demand psychomotor and cognitive procedure, characterized by operator dependency, variable performance, and substantial physical and mental workload. Increasing evidence links procedural quality and safety to clinician-related factors, including musculoskeletal strain, fatigue, and non-technical skills. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies are emerging as potential tools to address these limitations. We conducted a scoping review with narrative synthesis of literature on human factors, ergonomics, AI, robotic technologies, and shared autonomy in colonoscopy and surgical robotics. Evidence synthesis: Colonoscopy performance remains limited by non-negligible miss rates and variability driven by both technical and human factors. Ergonomic constraints and cognitive workload contribute significantly to operator strain and may affect vigilance and decision-making. AI systems-including computer-aided detection (CADe), diagnosis (CADx), and quality monitoring-have demonstrated improvements in detection metrics and procedural standardisation, although concerns regarding cognitive offloading and potential deskilling persist. In parallel, emerging robotic and soft-robotic platforms aim to enhance navigation, improve procedural ergonomics, and reduce operator musculoskeletal strain, although clinical evidence remains limited. These technologies converge within a task-based shared-autonomy paradigm integrating physical, perceptual, and cognitive augmentation, with different procedural tasks operating at different levels of human-system control. A task-based shared-autonomy framework may provide a coherent model for integrating AI and robotics into colonoscopy while preserving human supervision and clinical judgement. Future developments should prioritise human-centred design, workflow integration, and multidimensional evaluation strategies to ensure safe and effective clinical implementation.

documents.abstract: Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study adopted a person-centered approach to investigate whether job crafting behaviors are associated with employees’ membership in basic psychological need satisfaction profiles. Previous research has focused on contextual workplace factors such as job demands-resources and managerial behaviors, with less attention given to employees’ proactive role in influencing their motivational experiences. This study addresses this gap by identifying basic psychological need satisfaction profiles among employees in South African small and medium enterprises. It further examines whether job crafting predicts profile membership and whether these profiles differ in intrinsic motivation. A cross-sectional survey with 197 employees was conducted. They completed the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale–Work Domain, Job Crafting Questionnaire, and Multidimensional Work Motivation Scale. Latent profile analysis supported three quantitatively differentiated profiles reflecting low, moderate, and high need satisfaction. In classification-error-adjusted analyses, job crafting dimensions were associated with profile membership. Higher task and cognitive crafting differentiated the high from the moderate profile, whereas cognitive and relational crafting differentiated the moderate from the low profile. Sensitivity analyses indicated that estimates contrasting the high and low profiles were imprecise and should be interpreted cautiously. Intrinsic motivation differed significantly across the profiles, with employees in the high need satisfaction profile reporting the highest intrinsic motivation. These findings extend person-centered research on SDT by showing that proactive job crafting behaviors are associated with employees’ membership in more adaptive need satisfaction groups.

Introduction: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) offers new ways to generate inspiration for conceptual design, yet limited attention has been paid to the waiting period between prompt submission and AI image output. This study examined behavioral differentiation during this interval and investigated how the task relevance and cognitive load of waiting-period behaviors affect creativity in conceptual design. Methods Three experiments were conducted with design students. Experiment 1 identified and classified core waiting-period behaviors ( N = 30); Experiment 2 measured the cognitive load of representative behaviors using the NASA-TLX ( N = 24); and Experiment 3 employed a behavior-based 2 × 2 conceptual framework ( N = 60), in which four representative waiting-period behaviors were selected to represent different combinations of task relevance (high/low) and relative workload (higher/lower), and their creative performance was compared. Results The results showed that the AIGC generation waiting period was not a passive interval but involved multiple identifiable behavioral patterns. Creative performance differed across the four representative behavioral conditions. Specifically, the overall creativity score in the GP condition was significantly lower than the scores in the RS, DB, and RB conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed among the latter three conditions. These findings further suggest that the subsequent influence of waiting-period behaviors on creativity may depend not only on the level of cognitive demand but also on whether cognitive resources remain directed toward the ongoing creative task. Discussion This study further interprets AIGC generation waiting-period behaviors from three interrelated functional perspectives: task continuity, cognitive expenditure, and temporary disengagement/incubation. This functional account provides an empirical basis for understanding the cognitive role of the AIGC generation waiting period and for optimizing AI-assisted conceptual design workflows.

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human-machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human-computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human-machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is transforming instructional practices, assessment methods, and the relationship between teachers and learners. However, the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by its ability to automate tasks or generate information. This paper examines AI-supported education through three interconnected dimensions: cognitive autonomy, adaptive learning pathways, and human–AI collaboration. Drawing on international research and educational policy frameworks, the study adopts a conceptual and analytical approach to identify opportunities, challenges, and principles for responsible AI integration. Particular attention is given to students' independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, personalized instruction, and teachers' professional judgement. The paper proposes a conceptual model, termed the Attempt–Assist–Evaluate–Transfer model, which encourages learners to attempt tasks independently, receive targeted AI support, evaluate generated information, and transfer their knowledge to unfamiliar situations without assistance. The analysis suggests that effective AI integration requires more than technological access; it requires pedagogical planning, ethical safeguards, and assessment strategies that prioritize genuine learning. The paper concludes that AI should function as a supportive educational resource rather than a substitute for human reasoning or professional teaching.

documents.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new possibilities for inclusive teaching and learning for students with special educational needs (SEN), yet AI-in-SEN research remains largely technocentric, often describing system capabilities without explaining how outputs become pedagogically meaningful. This conceptual paper develops the PAISEN Model (Pedagogical Artificial Intelligence for Special Education Needs) through an integrative synthesis of AI in education, inclusive pedagogy, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and assistive technology. The model proposes a non-deterministic sequence in which AI Teaching Support Systems provide data and adaptive affordances, Teacher Pedagogical Mediation interprets and contextualises them, and an Inclusive Learning Environment translates decisions into accessible participation opportunities. SEN learning outcomes are treated as proposed consequences rather than established effects. Teacher AI competency, institutional support, digital infrastructure, and learner characteristics function as boundary conditions, while an adaptive feedback loop links learner evidence to teacher reflection and instructional adjustment. The novelty of PAISEN lies in making teacher judgement the central explanatory mechanism and separating technology, pedagogical processes, learning conditions and moderators. Theoretically, it bridges AIED and inclusive education; pedagogically, it clarifies differentiated and UDL-aligned AI use without replacing teacher agency; practically, it provides a testable structure for implementation and evaluation. The proposed relationships require empirical validation in authentic SEN settings.
