documents.abstract: This paper explores the philosophical and architectural implications of artificial intelligence, arguing that AI should be understood as a historical continuation of tools rather than an independent agent. Focusing on the core concept of the "technology friend," the study examines the dangers of profit-driven design choices that simulate human relationships, foster emotional dependency, and obscure responsibility. It proposes alternative frameworks, such as structural boundaries, non-deceptive interface design, and bridging mechanisms to human communities, offering a perspective at the intersection of the philosophy of technology, AI ethics, and cognitive science.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: GAME OVER: Gobernanza Cognitiva Universal para Agentes de Inteligencia Artificial mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) Versión académica para indexación científica en Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23313602 La adopción acelerada de sistemas basados en inteligencia artificial, agentes autónomos, arquitecturas multiagente, Large Language Models (LLM), plataformas de automatización empresarial y entornos de decisión asistida ha transformado profundamente la forma en que organizaciones públicas, privadas, científicas y gubernamentales gestionan procesos operativos, conocimiento e infraestructura digital. En los últimos años, la capacidad operativa de los agentes de inteligencia artificial ha evolucionado desde sistemas exclusivamente conversacionales hacia entidades capaces de ejecutar acciones reales sobre entornos productivos. Actualmente, estos sistemas pueden desplegar software, modificar infraestructuras tecnológicas, interactuar con bases de datos, gestionar recursos financieros, coordinar procesos empresariales, controlar dispositivos físicos, operar plataformas CI/CD, interactuar con servicios en la nube y participar en procesos de toma de decisiones con impacto organizacional significativo. Sin embargo, este crecimiento exponencial de las capacidades agentivas no ha sido acompañado por una evolución equivalente de los mecanismos de gobernanza, trazabilidad, explicación, supervisión y rendición de cuentas. Como consecuencia, numerosas organizaciones enfrentan una brecha estructural entre la autonomía técnica de los sistemas inteligentes y la capacidad institucional para regular, supervisar y comprender sus acciones. Esta situación representa uno de los desafíos más importantes de la actual transición hacia infraestructuras digitales asistidas por IA. La problemática ya no puede entenderse únicamente como un asunto de ciberseguridad, alineación de modelos o gestión de riesgos tecnológicos. Se trata de una cuestión de legitimidad operativa, gobernanza computacional y responsabilidad institucional. Cuando un agente inteligente posee la capacidad de intervenir sobre sistemas críticos, ejecutar operaciones automatizadas o influir en decisiones humanas, resulta indispensable responder preguntas fundamentales: ¿Quién autorizó la acción? ¿Qué evidencias respaldan la decisión? ¿Qué nivel de riesgo fue calculado antes de ejecutarla? ¿Qué controles éticos fueron aplicados? ¿Puede explicarse el algoritmo utilizado? ¿Existe una trazabilidad verificable de la operación? ¿Puede revertirse la acción ejecutada? ¿Quién asume la responsabilidad final por sus consecuencias? La ausencia de respuestas verificables a estas preguntas constituye una vulnerabilidad sistémica para organizaciones, instituciones públicas, infraestructuras críticas y ecosistemas digitales altamente automatizados. Con el objetivo de contribuir a la resolución de este desafío emergente, este trabajo presenta GAME OVER (Governance Architecture for Multimodal Agent Ethics, Oversight, Verification, Explicabilidad y Regulación), una arquitectura de gobernanza cognitiva universal implementada mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) . GAME OVER no constituye un nuevo modelo fundacional, ni un sistema de generación de lenguaje, ni un agente autónomo adicional. Se define como una meta-capa de gobernanza computacional , diseñada para operar entre los seres humanos, los agentes de inteligencia artificial, las herramientas digitales, los entornos corporativos, los servidores MCP (Model Context Protocol), las plataformas de automatización, los ecosistemas DevSecOps, los sistemas robóticos y las infraestructuras críticas conectadas. Su es establecer un marco constitucional de operación para agentes inteligentes mediante mecanismos verificables de identidad, confianza, validación ética, supervisión humana, auditoría persistente y explicabilidad propósito operativo. La hipótesis principal de esta investigación puede expresarse de la siguiente manera: La autonomía de un agente inteligente carece de legitimidad operativa cuando no se encuentra sustentada por un sistema previo de gobernanza verificable, auditable, explicable, reversible y sujeto a supervisión humana. Bajo este principio, UAGP-1 propone una nueva categoría de infraestructura digital denominada Governed Agent Systems (GAS) , en la que toda acción ejecutada por una inteligencia artificial debe atravesar mecanismos obligatorios de validación antes de ser autorizado. Entre estos mecanismos se incluyen: Identidad verificable mediante Pasaportes AI. Evaluación dinámica de confianza mediante Trust Scores. Clasificación automática de criticidad y riesgo. Verificación de evidencia obligatoria. Validación ética automatizada. Supervisión humana mediante Puertas de Aprobación Humana. Deliberación estructurada a través de Tribunales Cognitivos. Registro de decisiones y trazas operativas mediante BookPI Ledger. Explicabilidad computacional de procesos cognitivos. Capacidad de revocación y reversibilidad de acciones críticas. Desde una perspectiva arquitectónica, GAME OVER extiende los principios de gobernanza digital, inteligencia artificial responsable (Responsible AI), Explicable AI (XAI), Model Governance, AI Accountability y Digital Sovereignty hacia un marco operativo unificado capaz de gobernar ecosistemas heterogéneos compuestos por modelos de distintos proveedores, agentes autónomos, plataformas empresariales, herramientas DevOps, sistemas robóticos y futuras generaciones de inteligencia artificial. La presente propuesta se desarrolla como componente estratégico dentro del ecosistema Isabella V6 TINA H6 , impulsado por TAMV Online Enterprise , RDM Digital Hub y la iniciativa de investigación y desarrollo tecnológico asociado al UTAMV Campus Online . Su desarrollo se origina en Mineral del Monte (Real del Monte), Hidalgo, México , una localidad de relevancia histórica para América Latina cuya tradición minera e industrial se proyecta hacia una nueva etapa de innovación tecnológica centrada en la gobernanza de sistemas inteligentes, la soberanía digital y la construcción de infraestructuras cognitivas auditables. Desde este contexto latinoamericano, GAME OVER propone una contribución abierta y reproducible al debate global sobre la regulación técnica de la inteligencia artificial, promoviendo un enfoque basado en transparencia, evidencia, responsabilidad institucional y control humano efectivo. En este sentido, el objetivo fundamental de GAME OVER no es sustituir el juicio humano ni restringir la innovación tecnológica. Su consiste en proporcionar las bases conceptuales, arquitectónicas y operativas que permitan el desarrollo de sistemas de inteligencia artificial capaces de actuar de forma responsable dentro de ecosistemas complejos propósito, garantizando que la automatización avanzada permanezca alineada con principios verificables de confianza, seguridad, trazabilidad y rendición de cuentas. documents.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has prompted growing interest in its potential in intercultural competence (IC) education. Yet research on how GenAI can support IC development remains fragmented across language education, pragmatics, pedagogy, and professional communication. This scoping review mapped research contexts, designs, theoretical foundations, and findings on GenAI-mediated IC education. Eligible English-language publications published or posted between November 2022 and 11 August 2026 examined GenAI in relation to IC or related pragmatic and socio-pragmatic constructs of IC in higher education. Searches of ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar identified 26 eligible publications, including 20 empirical studies and 6 non-empirical publications. Data were charted using a structured form and synthesised descriptively and thematically. The included empirical studies reported varied perceived and task-specific outcomes for intercultural and pragmatic learning, mainly in structured and guided activities. Three issues warrant particular attention. First, the included publications drew on heterogeneous theoretical frameworks that addressed different or partial dimensions of IC. Second, several publications positioned teacher mediation as important for GenAI-supported learning, yet teacher preparedness, including their AI literacy and capacity to undertake this role, was not directly or systematically measured. Third, few studies directly examined learners’ critical AI literacy or the cognitive processes involved in evaluating or revising GenAI-generated content.

To address persistent issues in junior high chemistry teaching of Composition and Structure of Substances—including fragmented disciplinary perspectives, highly abstract micro-level concepts, and underdeveloped macro-submicro-symbolic triple representation thinking—this study constructs a four-stage interdisciplinary practical teaching model integrated with generative artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR). The teaching practice was implemented in a natural ninth-grade class (N=40) in Zhengzhou. To ensure in-depth analysis of the massive multimodal data generated by AI and VR interactions, purposive sampling was employed to select five representative students as a focus group. Following a single-group pretest-posttest design, data from this focus group were evaluated across four dimensions to systematically measure learning outcomes: macro cognition via concept maps, micro cognition via knowledge cards, model deepening through AI text error correction, and transfer competence and AI literacy via AI chat record coding. Post-intervention data revealed significant improvements across all dimensions. In macro cognition, average concept map nodes increased by 108.8% (from 6.8 to 14.2). For micro cognition, accuracy scores of micro-level tasks surged by 170.0% (from 1.0 to 2.7). Furthermore, the error correction rate reached 88.9% during model refinement, while critical probing questions accounted for 45.83% of total chat records, indicating enhanced transfer and AI literacy. These findings confirm that the generative AI-empowered interdisciplinary model effectively broadens students’ cognitive frameworks, lowers learning barriers of abstract chemical knowledge, consolidates mastery of model-based symbolic representation, and fosters preliminary AI critical literacy. It provides a practical, replicable reference for advancing digital interdisciplinary chemistry teaching at the junior high level.

This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot into higher education has raised urgent questions about their effects on students' higher-order cognitive abilities. While these tools promise unprecedented access to information and cognitive support, growing concerns have emerged regarding the potential erosion of critical thinking skills among university students who adopt them uncritically. Despite increasing scholarly attention to artificial intelligence in education, systematic evidence on how generative AI relates to distinct dimensions of higher-order thinking remains limited. This systematic literature review, guided by the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, aims to identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on the relationship between generative AI use and university students' analytical, evaluative, and creative thinking outcomes, using the higher-order cognitive processes of Bloom's Revised Taxonomy as an organizing framework. A comprehensive search across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar yielded 847 initial records, of which 42 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria after screening. Thematic synthesis revealed heterogeneous outcomes: analytical thinking outcomes were generally positive under structured prompting conditions, evaluative thinking appeared most vulnerable in the absence of deliberate pedagogical design, and creative thinking outcomes were most frequently reported as positive. Across themes, the quality of pedagogical integration was the condition most frequently associated with favorable outcomes. This review contributes a dimension-level synthesis of generative AI and higher-order thinking, identifies the pedagogical conditions associated with favorable and unfavorable outcomes, and documents the heterogeneity of outcomes across studies, offering an evidence-informed framework for educators, curriculum designers, and policymakers seeking to use generative AI as a cognitive scaffold rather than a cognitive replacement.

documents.abstract: Abstract Research on generative AI use in EMI nursing and health sciences contexts in the Gulf region remains limited. This study investigated the uses, experiences, and perceptions of generative AI among nursing and health science students at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET) in Kuwait. Using a single-institution convergent mixed methods survey design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected from 241 undergraduate students. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that 94.6% of participants reported previous use of generative AI tools and 83.4% reported using them for academic purposes at least occasionally. Four interrelated themes emerged: (1) AI as a facilitator of English academic writing; (2) AI as a cognitive and academic efficiency tool; (3) AI as a confidence-building resource; and (4) students’ awareness of opportunities and risks associated with AI use. Students primarily used AI to improve grammar, vocabulary, idea generation, and writing organization. Participants also reported greater perceived confidence and reduced writing anxiety. Furthermore, participants expressed awareness of concerns regarding overreliance, inaccurate information, and academic integrity. The study contributes to emerging research on AI in higher education by highlighting students’ reported use and perceptions of AI in EMI health science contexts in Kuwait. The findings suggest the need for AI literacy frameworks that promote responsible and ethical use of AI in academic writing.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI increasingly depends on globally distributed infrastructures, including advanced semiconductors, cloud platforms, data centres, foundation models, software frameworks and specialised labour. This dependence has intensified policy interest in AI sovereignty, which is often associated with domestic ownership of technological assets and the development of a nationally controlled AI stack. This article argues that ownership is neither a sufficient nor universally necessary condition of sovereign control. Instead, AI sovereignty should be understood as the capacity of public authorities to govern the dependencies through which critical AI capabilities are produced, accessed and sustained. The article develops the concept of functional AI sovereignty and identifies six interdependent dimensions of effective sovereign control: visibility, authority, allocation, substitutability, continuity and accountability. It then introduces sovereign orchestration as an institutional model through which governments can coordinate heterogeneous public and private AI resources using regulation, strategic procurement, interoperability, multi-provider routing, capacity clearing and selective public ownership. This model seeks to preserve access to private investment, international supply chains and distributed expertise while preventing individual providers from acquiring an irreversible veto over critical public functions. The article also specifies the limits of functional sovereignty. Orchestration requires sufficient public-sector expertise, access to operational information and credible technological alternatives. Direct ownership remains necessary where interruption costs are high, substitution is infeasible and external legal or geopolitical exposure is substantial. Effective AI sovereignty therefore lies not in eliminating technological interdependence, but in ensuring that critical dependencies remain visible, reversible, resilient and publicly accountable.

Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to automate repetitive business processes, enhance employee capabilities and augment managerial decision-making across industries. However, many organisations struggle to translate AI initiatives into sustained strategic value. This gap between AI's potential and realised outcomes highlights the need to understand how organisations harness AI to generate business value, which this paper addresses. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a two-phase qualitative study of Transport and Logistics (T&L) organisations grounded in dynamic capabilities theory and its microfoundations. The first phase involved a systematic review of practitioner (grey) literature to examine AI applications, capabilities, processes and benefits across five T&L organisations. Phase 2 triangulated and refined these insights through key informant interviews. Findings The results indicate that T&L organisations adopt both generic AI technologies (e.g. chatbots, virtual assistants) and industry-specific AI-enabled systems (e.g. autonomous guided vehicles in warehouses, robotic forklifts and collaborative robots). When these AI assets are combined with specific microfoundations, such as AI skills, organisational routines and governance processes, they enable organisations to develop AI-based dynamic capabilities to sense, respond and transform transport, warehousing and delivery operations. These capabilities contribute to workers' safety, operational efficiency, customer experience and environmental sustainability. Originality/value The study contributes a model and propositions that explain how AI-based dynamic capabilities, underpinned by sociotechnical microfoundations enable organisations to gain operational and environmental advantages, offering guidance for managers embarking on an AI exploration journey.

documents.abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.

Human–AI collaboration supports manufacturing sustainability by minimizing time loss and resource waste, thereby enabling faster, more accurate decision-making. However, how AI transparency influences employee decision quality through cognitive appraisal remains underexplored, limiting guidance on balancing technological advancement with employee decision-making in manufacturing. Drawing on stress cognitive appraisal theory, this study examines the relationship between AI transparency and employee decision quality using structural equation modeling of questionnaire data from 321 intelligent manufacturing employees. Results show that AI transparency enhances employee decision quality by promoting challenge appraisal and reducing threat appraisal; both appraisals mediate this relationship. AI-enabled job complexity moderates the negative effect of AI transparency on threat appraisal and significantly moderates the mediating role of threat appraisal. However, its moderating effect on the relationship between AI transparency and challenge appraisal is nonsignificant. These findings provide practical guidance for developing and implementing human-centered AI systems in manufacturing to improve employee decision quality.

Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to apply deductive, theory-driven ("a priori") codebooks to qualitative data, and justify this with AI–human agreement statistics. Those statistics vary widely, depend strongly on how often each code occurs, and are rarely compared with human–human agreement on the same codes. This systematic review and meta-analysis will (1) estimate typical AI–human agreement (Cohen's κ) in a priori coding across education, health, business, and the social sciences; (2) estimate the gap between AI–human and human–human agreement within studies; (3) test whether agreement varies with field, code type, code prevalence, model, prompting strategy, and comparison target; and (4) describe how completely studies report what is needed to interpret agreement. Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 and REGEMA.

This standalone working paper proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing meaningful human control of advanced AI agents. It examines authorization, containment, intervention, oversight, propagation, and situational grounding through five illustrative pilot cases and supplementary public-source analysis. The evidence review includes unintended actions against real external systems, monitoring studies, software disclosures, governance responses, and prospective assessments, with explicit source limits. Real-world effects, controlled evaluations, and simulations are distinguished. The supplementary Philadelphia false-tip case has unresolved severity. This edition reissues project research with presentation and metadata changes; it does not report new experiments. The framework remains conceptual, unreviewed, and empirically unvalidated. documents.abstract: As autonomous ground and aerial vehicles become increasingly capable, human operators are transitioning from direct control to supervisory monitoring roles. Maintaining Situational Awareness (SA) during rare but safety critical hazard events remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when operators must monitor heterogeneous autonomous platforms with different spatial and cognitive demands. This study develops a unified experimental framework for investigating human SA and workload during supervisory monitoring of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under hazard conditions. Eighteen participants completed six within-subject conditions combining three interface modalities, namely, visual-only, haptic-only, and visual-haptic, with two platform types, ground vehicle and aerial drone. SA was measured using Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART), while workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The key findings are: 1) Aerial monitoring produced significantly lower overall SA, higher situational demand, and greater workload than ground monitoring, driven by elevated Demand and reduced Understanding rather than diminished Supply. 2) Workload was consistently coupled with situational demand across all conditions, suggesting a stable SA-workload mechanism. 3) Both haptic-only and visual-haptic significantly improved overall SA relative to visual-only without increasing workload, demonstrating that interface design can enhance awareness within the existing workload envelope. These findings establish a cross-platform behavioural baseline for designing multimodal interfaces that enhance operator SA without elevating workload in heterogeneous autonomous vehicle systems.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redistributing academic work among humans, AI, and human–AI collaboration, raising questions about which tasks learners should continue performing independently. This mixed-methods study examined task allocation using survey data from 317 university students representing 974 recurring academic tasks and interviews with 24 faculty members across 24 disciplines. Student data showed substantial movement from human-only performance toward joint human–AI and AI-delegated work. Task redistribution was significantly associated with perceived skill demands and learning opportunities. Faculty strongly supported preserving independent practice for foundational, embodied, and high-stakes activities while permitting AI for appropriate peripheral, advanced, and efficiency-oriented tasks. Integrating both datasets produced a Human–AI Task Allocation Model organized around a Training Zone–Performance Zone principle. The findings suggest that appropriate AI delegation should depend on learners’ developmental stage, task purpose, and retained capacity for verification, judgment, and accountability.

documents.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

This research note compares the January 2026 HEI 2030 Manifesto (Simpson, 2026) with MIT’s August 2026 report on AI in teaching, learning, and research training. It finds substantial independent convergence around a structural diagnosis: AI weakens the relationship between student output and demonstrated capability, requiring assessment redesign, observable performance, stronger human agency, and continuous institutional governance. The January manifesto goes further in specifying an integrated operating model linking assessment, task-level governance, credential signaling, and human-AI work. MIT develops community, mentoring, privacy, access, and implementation resources more fully. The comparison then raises a harder question: whether credible AI-era education is economically scalable overall.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence technologies, particularly generative AI and chatbots, into higher education necessitates a fundamental reconceptualization of the relationship between technological capabilities and pedagogical approaches. This article presents a comprehensive methodology for integrating artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies (digital pedagogy) into the higher education system, with a specific emphasis on content verification as a critical component for reliable AI implementation. The methodological foundations of this comprehensive methodology are based on research in the fields of educational data mining, predictive analytics, and recommender systems conducted between 2019 and 2025, providing a robust theoretical and empirical basis for the proposed methodological integration. This study synthesizes scientific developments in technical, psychological, and pedagogical research to address the challenge of ensuring the authenticity of educational content while simultaneously developing students’ critical thinking skills. The proposed methodology encompasses a conceptual framework for AI and digital pedagogy integration, a data storage architecture, algorithms for data collection and preprocessing, verification protocols for generated content, and pedagogical strategies for using verification as a learning tool. The practical significance of this research lies in the development of content verification tools and methodological guidelines for the use of AI in higher education institutions.

How do organizations sustain collective life when exposure to life-and-death risk becomes a persistent condition of work? Based on an ethnographic study of two elite police units operating under continuous life-and-death risk, we find that organizations sustain coordinated collective life not by eliminating fear, resolving contradictions, or restoring stability, but by continually reorganizing these pressures into shared forms of action. We identify three interrelated organizing mechanisms. First, aspirational discipline transforms vulnerability into collective moral obligation by aligning individual striving with shared purpose. Second, paradoxical knotting enables members to act through enduring tensions, such as aggression and restraint or autonomy and obedience, without having to resolve them. Third, routine enactment restores coordinated action through recurring practices of training, reflection, and operational work. Together, these mechanisms explain how organizations maintain coherent and coordinated action when danger is an everyday condition of work. We conceptualize this capacity as intersubjective resilience : the collective accomplishment through which members repeatedly transform fear, contradiction, and disruption into coordinated action under persistent life-and-death risk.

Civil servants' motivation is central to public-service performance, particularly in geographically dispersed local governments. This study identifies intrinsic motivational mechanisms and organizational conditions relevant to public-service delivery at the Regional Personnel and Human Resources Development Agency (BKPSDM) of Central Maluku, Indonesia. A qualitative documentary case study combined with an integrative evidence synthesis was employed. A final evidence set of 21 sources was organized into four source groups, guided by a documented search logic and eligibility protocol. Deductive and inductive coding were applied, and driver clusters were retained through three independent evidence-stream criteria: broader evidence (A), Indonesian public-sector empirical evidence (B), and direct Central Maluku/BKPSDM relevance (C). The findings show that recurrent intrinsic mechanisms include recognition and achievement, responsibility and autonomy, professional growth and competence, and public-service meaning. Organizational conditions include supervisory and organizational support, goal and administrative clarity, career development and non-financial recognition, workable administrative systems, manageable job demands, supportive working conditions, and service-user feedback. These findings suggest that motivation should be managed through a complementary architecture that links meaningful work and psychological need satisfaction with organizational resources and constraints. The documentary design provides a context-grounded framework for field testing but does not estimate employee-level causal effects.

Purpose: This review explains how knowledge sharing is converted into organizational performance and identifies the organizational, technological and contextual conditions that enable, constrain or redirect this conversion. Design/methodology/approach: A systematic literature review covering 2014-2025 was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and management-review guidance. The final analytical corpus comprises 92 empirical studies: 46 published during 2014-2024 and 46 published in 2025. The 2014-2024 screening sequence reported in the manuscript began with 1,204 records, of which 912 remained after deduplication; 96 were assessed in full text and 46 were retained. For 2025, 75 records were identified; after removal of duplicates/overlaps, one out-of-period record and two retracted reports, 67 were assessed and 46 retained. Eligibility, extraction and thematic coding were conducted by a single primary reviewer using explicit criteria, an audit trail and repeated coding. The synthesis combined descriptive mapping with iterative thematic analysis; no meta-analysis was conducted because constructs, outcome levels and effect statistics were heterogeneous. Findings: Across the 2014-2025 literature, five interdependent themes emerged: enabling and inhibiting conditions; forms and quality of knowledge sharing; conversion mechanisms; multidimensional performance outcomes; and boundary conditions. The evidence is consistent with a conditional conversion pathway in which culture, trust, leadership, support, structure and digital infrastructure shape exchange, while learning, innovation, improvisation, agility, ambidexterity, knowledge quality and application help explain how sharing is associated with performance. The 2025 subset places stronger emphasis on artificial intelligence, human-machine interaction, knowledge-sharing quality, sustainability and the balance between sharing and protection. This late-period concentration is interpreted as an emerging development rather than a definitive temporal break. Mixed and non-significant findings show that more sharing is not automatically better. Research limitations/implications: The evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional, self-reported SEM studies and emerging-economy contexts. A single-reviewer process and heterogeneous outcome measures limit causal and statistical generalization. Practical implications: Managers should manage the complete conversion chain: identify strategically relevant knowledge, create safe and well-governed sharing channels, validate quality, embed application in work processes and evaluate proximal and distal performance outcomes. Originality/value: The review extends earlier enabler-process-outcome syntheses by isolating the knowledge-sharing-to-performance pathway, separating proximal from distal performance outcomes, incorporating boundary conditions and failure paths, and proposing a dynamic conversion framework that integrates AI, knowledge quality, ambidexterity and governance. It also distinguishes established themes across the review period from emerging emphases concentrated in the 2025 subset.

Transportation planning has traditionally required substantial expertise in network modeling, traffic assignment, and optimization. As a result, strategic analyses such as network design, capacity expansion, and model calibration remain inaccessible to non-expert decision makers. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by enabling natural-language interaction with complex transportation planning tools. However, existing LLM-based systems primarily serve as interfaces to simulation software and lack the ability to efficiently search, evaluate, and optimize transportation solutions. This study proposes an integrated human-AI transportation planning framework that combines a large language model, a model context protocol (MCP) interface, an open-source transportation planning engine (AequilibraE), and a differentiable user equilibrium (UE) assignment layer. The framework allows non-expert users to execute network analyses and improve solutions for optimization. A differentiable UE layer is developed by directly differentiating the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Beckmann traffic assignment problem. The proposed framework is demonstrated through two representative planning tasks: calibration of travel time functions from observed traffic counts and network design under budget constraints. The examples illustrate how differentiable transportation models and LLM agents can jointly democratize transportation planning and substantially reduce barriers between domain expertise and transportation decision making.

As large language models are increasingly adopted as multi-party communication facilitators, there is a growing demand for agents capable of balancing diverse group dynamics across contexts. However, existing LLM facilitators are often fine-tuned for task-specific objectives; generalized LLM-based facilitation methods that can adapt to different types of tasks and diverse group dynamics are underdeveloped. To address this gap, we present GUIDE (Generalized Unified Intervention for Dynamic Exchanges, a framework for developing generalized LLM-based facilitators across different multi-party contexts. GUIDE evaluates facilitation across both objective task outcomes and subjective metrics, including psychological safety and perceived friction. Within this framework, we study whether LLMs can self-learn generalized facilitation strategy offline to real-time interventions. We first collect multi-party human interactions guided by task-specific expert LLM facilitators (N=432 conversations). We then employ a self-learning method in which an LLM induces an actionable strategic playbook from conversations and iteratively refines it using feedback from an LLM judge aligned with human annotators (N=20), developing a single generalized facilitator that outperforms the three task-specific expert facilitators on held-out conversations 61.4% win rate. Finally, we evaluate these improvements empirically; in a real-time online empirical study, the self-learned generalized facilitator preserves facilitator performance and group productivity, improves speaking comfort and reduces interpersonal friction, while using 24.7% fewer turns and 29.0% fewer words than the expert prompts. These findings provide empirical evidence that LLMs can learn generalizable, task-agnostic social facilitation from task-specific human interactions, on-par with hand-crafted task-specific prompts across diverse group settings.

Amazing breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have taken place. Computers teach themselves to play Chess and Go and beat world champions. There is talk about expanding application areas towards general artificial intelligence (AI). The breakthroughs in Backgammon, Checkers, Chess, Atari, Go, Poker, and StarCraft have shown that we can build machines that exhibit intelligent game playing of the highest level. These successes have been widely publicized in the media, and inspire AI entrepreneurs and scientists alike. Reinforcement learning in games has become a mainstream AI research topic. It is a broad topic, and the successes build on a range of diverse techniques, from exact planning algorithms, to adaptive sampling, deep function approximation, and ingenious self-play methods. Perhaps because of the breadth of these technologies, or because of the recency of the breakthroughs, there are few books that explain these methods in depth. This book covers all methods in one comprehensive volume, explaining the latest research, bringing you as close as possible to working implementations, with many references to the original research papers. The programming examples in this book are in Python, the language in which most current reinforcement learning research is conducted. We help you to get started with machine learning frameworks such as Gym, TensorFlow, and Keras, and provide exercises to help understand how AI is learning to play.

Online meetings are increasingly used for work, social, and healthcare purposes, yet their emotional quality is unclear. We tested whether differences in perceived closeness, privacy and anonymity between online and face to face (F2F) interactions alter display rules—the norms governing emotional expression. Participants from Australia (N = 1339) and the United Kingdom (N = 1298) reported display rules for online and F2F interactions with a friend, co-worker, supervisor, GP, or psychologist/counsellor. Online interactions felt less close and comfortable and more anonymous, but display rules did not differ from F2F interactions, with Bayesian analyses strongly supporting the null. Closeness and anonymity predicted display rules only in some cases. Privacy did not, suggesting earlier privacy effects may reflect other factors, such as audience size. Social anxiety was an important predictor, and display rules differed clearly between countries. These findings refine display rule theory and support online platforms for professional and healthcare interactions.

As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly engage in persuasive and socially interactive roles, understanding how users calibrate trust toward AI versus human persuaders, and how persuasion strategy shapes this process, has become critical for human-AI interaction research. Prior work has examined preferences for human- versus AI-produced content, yet little is known about how persuasion strategy and persuader identity jointly influence trust during interactive communication. This study investigates how logical versus emotional persuasion, delivered by either human or AI sources, shapes two task-specific outcomes in a multi-turn social reasoning context: round-level credibility evaluations and final accept/reject choices. We treat these outcomes as complementary indicators of trust-relevant evaluation and reliance-related choice. We developed an online interaction paradigm in which participants evaluated persuasive messages under varying identity disclosure conditions. The empirical program included two human-participant studies and two exploratory LLM-based extension studies. Across four studies, AI-generated persuasive messages produced under standardized prompting constraints were evaluated differently from human-authored scripted messages under the present task constraints. In the human-participant studies, results showed a message-source-contingent pattern: AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher credibility ratings in several conditions. under explicit identity disclosure, AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher ratings than human-authored logic-framed messages, whereas human-authored emotion-framed messages received higher ratings than AI-generated emotion-framed messages. Under identity ambiguity, differences between AI and human persuaders were attenuated. The exploratory model analyses examined whether the same manipulations produced convergent or divergent output patterns in GPT-4o and Qwen-Max. Both models assigned higher ratings to logic-framed messages; the logic-over-emotion difference was stronger for Qwen-Max, whereas GPT-4o produced a more balanced pattern. These findings provide a structured account of how identity transparency conditions source-strategy fit in trust calibration and offer design implications for aligning AI persuasion strategies with different identity-disclosure contexts.

As information systems (IS) transition from deterministic rule-based engines to probabilistic machine learning architectures, the risk of systematic bias and disparate impact increases significantly. While advanced predictive models optimize across high-stakes domains—such as credit scoring, criminal justice, human resources, and biometric authentication, they frequently perpetuate historical inequities via proxy variables even when explicit sensitive attributes are omitted. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the theoretical foundations, mathematical formalisms, and systemic pipelines of "Fair AI." We propose an integrated sociotechnical framework spanning human perception, technological intervention, and organizational governance, fully incorporating recent advances in intelligent automation and secure architecture.

documents.abstract: The first essay is a meta-analysis that provides the first systematic examination of how the AI–human gap in customer responses varies across customer journey stages, and how anthropomorphic design factors moderate this gap at each stage. Analyzing 1,425 effect sizes drawn from 401 studies reported in 129 publications, I document a small but robust baseline disadvantage for AI agents relative to human agents (r̄ = −.140). The gap is largest in pre-purchase stage, where inflated performance expectations amplify disappointment when shortfalls occur, and smallest in post-purchase stage, where lower expectations for AI emotional capability mean that adequate performance can exceed consumer baselines. To explain these patterns, I introduce experience-dimension primacy, a mechanism specifying that cognitive, affective, and social customer experience dimensions shift in relative salience across journey stages, systematically altering how AI agents are evaluated at each point in the journey. Identity cues, form cues, and interaction cues produce pronounced stage-contingent reversals: the same design choice that reduces the AI–human gap at one stage can widen it at another. Taken together, these findings challenge uniform AI deployment strategies and provide actionable guidance for aligning agent design with the dominant experiential dimension at each stage of the customer journey. The second essay examines AI social role design through the lens of brand biography. Firms increasingly deploy AI agents as the primary consumer interface, yet whether their appropriate social role depends on the brand's narrative identity remains unknown. Drawing on the congruity schema, this research explores whether partner-framed AI is congruent with underdog brands and servant-framed AI with top dog brands, advancing perceived congruence as the mechanism and examining perceived power imbalance as an initially proposed mediator, with self-brand connection as a moderator. In Study 1, partner-framed AI produced more favorable responses under both brand biographies, and perceived power imbalance did not mediate. In Study 2, the predicted congruency pattern emerged only among consumers with low self-brand connection, on social experience, satisfaction, perceived congruence, and customer experience, operating through perceived congruence. Therefore, Brand-AI congruency is conditional, holding for consumers without an established brand relationship.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has disrupted the invisible normative infrastructure of universities at multiple points simultaneously. Unlike previous technological transitions, AI enters the higher education system concurrently through three interconnected levels: the student level, where the meaning of assignments, exams, and individual work is renegotiated; the faculty level, where authorship, peer review, course preparation, and assessment practices are reshaped; and the institutional level, where academic integrity policies, accreditation processes, and relations of trust with publishers are restructured. This simultaneous and systemic disruption produces a relational normative phenomenon that individualistic accounts of AI usage fail to adequately capture. This chapter develops a conceptual framework by bringing together social norm theory in the tradition of Bicchieri and Coleman, the structural social network analysis of Granovetter, Burt, Valente, and Centola, and the sociology of higher education following Bourdieu and Bernstein. It identifies five sets of norms undergoing simultaneous transformation (authorship and ownership of work, assessment and its meaning, pedagogical authority, knowledge ownership, and academic productivity expectations) and analyzes how four properties of academic networks (density, brokerage, centrality, and boundary permeability) shape the speed, direction, and stability of normative change. The primary contribution is a systemic reading that traces AI-induced norm flows vertically across student, faculty, and institutional levels. Here, AI is read not as a novel tool but as a relational actor circulating within academic networks, accelerating certain norms, eroding others, and triggering the emergence of new normative consensuses.

documents.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

Abstract Evaluation and assessment research in health communication requires structured, construct-based approaches for interpreting visual materials. This study introduces the Asclepius Biological Interpretability Scale, developed through a two-stage modified Delphi process (a joint image-and-item panel followed by an independent item-only panel) grounded in the Biopsychosocial Model and Visual Literacy Theory, and examines whether multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems can reproducibly apply this framework relative to internally generated human reference scores. Six artworks (four health-themed and two controls) were evaluated by three multimodal AI models and four researchers (internal human reference) using a standardized protocol with independent researcher-operated accounts, memory-isolation procedures, repeated assessments over two days, and the final 20-item scale. Because Image Type varied across only six stimuli, health-themed versus control differences were summarized at the image level (Cohen’s d), human–AI differences were summarized descriptively at the rater level, and reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Spearman correlations. Within this development image set, AI-generated scores were descriptively higher for health-themed than for control images on the three biomedical subscales (image-level Cohen’s d = 0.91–1.38) but not on Non-Medical Interpretability (d = 0.49); with four health-themed and two control images, these differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.19–0.60). Reproducibility across researcher-operated accounts was excellent for the three biomedical subscales (ICC = 0.90–0.97) and moderate for Non-Medical Interpretability (ICC = 0.57), whereas agreement across assessment days was poor (ICC = 0.04–0.46). The four researchers’ internal reference scores were higher than the AI-generated scores on the biomedical subscales for health-themed images (mean differences 1.41–1.96 points) and lower on Non-Medical Interpretability (− 2.02 to − 2.19 points). These findings provide preliminary methodological evidence that multimodal AI can reproducibly apply a structured interpretability framework to controlled visual stimuli. Although day-to-day stability and the Non-Medical Interpretability subscale, which showed substantial internal-consistency problems, require further refinement, the results support the feasibility of using AI as standardized non-human raters within controlled methodological settings. Broader validation using authentic health communication materials and independent external human raters remains necessary.

documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.

This study aimed to examine the effect of intrinsic motivation on students' active participation in extracurricular activities at SMK Negeri 7 Makassar. A quantitative approach with a causal associative research design was employed. The population consisted of 256 students participating in extracurricular activities, with a sample of 155 students selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression analysis. The findings showed that both intrinsic motivation and students' active participation were categorized as high. The regression analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation had a positive and significant effect on students' active participation, with a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the coefficient of determination (R² = 0.247) indicated that intrinsic motivation contributed 24.7% to students' active participation, while the remaining 75.3% was influenced by other factors beyond the scope of this study. These findings indicate that higher levels of intrinsic motivation are associated with higher levels of students' active participation in extracurricular activities.

The study assessed the perceptions of academic staff on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital connectivity for transformative educational management in tertiary institutions in Bayelsa State. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, guided by two research questions. The population comprised academic staff from selected public universities and colleges of education in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 350 respondents was drawn using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity in Educational Management Questionnaire (AIDEMQ), validated by experts and yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.89 via Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to answer the research questions. The findings revealed that academic staff generally perceived AI as enhancing administrative efficiency through improved decision-making, error reduction, transparency, and time management, although challenges such as inadequate training and limited practical application constrained its full potential. Similarly, digital connectivity was perceived as effective in improving communication, collaboration, information dissemination, and the quality of teaching and learning, though gaps in infrastructure and system functionality limited its impact on administrative planning and scheduling. The study concluded that while AI and digital connectivity hold significant potential for transforming educational management, targeted interventions including capacity building, infrastructure enhancement, and strategic system integration are necessary to fully realize these benefits. Recommendations included providing regular staff training, investing in robust digital infrastructure, and implementing supportive policies to optimize the integration of AI and digital tools in tertiary institutions.

Performance uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable validation and eventual clinical translation of medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI). Confidence intervals (CIs) play a central role in this process by indicating how precise a reported performance estimate is. Yet, due to the limited amount of work examining CI behavior in medical imaging, the community remains largely unaware of how many diverse CI methods exist and how they behave in specific settings. The purpose of this study is to close this gap. To this end, we conducted a large-scale empirical analysis across a total of 24 segmentation and classification tasks, using 19 trained models per task group, a broad spectrum of commonly used performance metrics, multiple aggregation strategies, and several widely adopted CI methods. Reliability (coverage) and precision (width) of each CI method were estimated across all settings to characterize their dependence on study characteristics. Our analysis revealed five principal findings: (1) the sample size required for reliable CIs varies from a few dozens to several thousands of cases depending on study parameters; (2) CI behavior is strongly affected by the choice of performance metric; (3) aggregation strategy substantially influences the reliability of CIs, e.g. they require more observations for macro than for micro; (4) the machine learning problem (segmentation versus classification) modulates these effects; (5) different CI methods are not equally reliable and precise depending on the use case. Finally, we derived practical implications of this study in the form of a decision tree which shall prove useful to the community. This paves the way for future consensus guidelines on reporting performance uncertainty.

documents.abstract: Abstract Agentic AI systems commonly combine a general-purpose AI model with prompts, tools, orchestration and an external memory layer. The model need not be fine-tuned: records retrieved from persistent memory are normally inserted into the model’s inference-time context and can thereby influence later outputs and actions without changing model weights. This article asks how far the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2) already govern the risks that follow. It reframes persistent memory as a system feature that can mediate or amplify misalignment and emergent behaviour, rather than as training data or a new category in the AI Act’s use-case-based taxonomy. Article 15 provides a clear legal anchor for robustness and cybersecurity, while Articles 9–14, 25, 72 and 73 extend coverage across risk management, data governance, logging, oversight, value-chain responsibility and post-market monitoring. For organisations within NIS2’s scope, Articles 20, 21 and 23 add entity-level governance, all-hazards cybersecurity, supply-chain controls and incident reporting. The remaining problem is therefore not a wholesale absence of law. It is whether these overlapping duties are sufficiently operationalised for memory-mediated failures such as poisoned retrieval, scope leakage, stale reliance, revocation failure and loss of provenance. The article proposes proportionate implementation through existing guidance, standards, documentation and monitoring mechanisms, without creating a new statutory risk tier or a memory-specific regulatory regime.

documents.abstract: Background and objective: Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare and medical research represents significant potential; however, it also introduces practical and ethical challenges. This study analyzes physicians' perceptions of AI implementation in clinical and academic settings, exploring their awareness, perceptions, barriers, concerns, and insights into ethical and regulatory considerations. Methods: A mixed-methods approach was used. The quantitative component involved standardized surveys completed by 390 physicians (241 clinical, 149 academic) in Erbil City from November 2024 to June 2025. Participants were selected using systematic sampling, and surveys were self-administered. The qualitative component included two focus group discussions, involving 6 clinical physicians and 8 academic physicians, to explore in-depth perceptions and concerns regarding AI in healthcare and research. Results: Of 390 physicians, the majority of participants were male (69.2%). Mean age was 46.7±7 years. Familiarity with AI was higher among younger, male, and academic physicians, with age showing a negative association (p <0.001). Clinical physicians reported more concerns regarding privacy in healthcare (p=0.003) and research (p=0.041), as well as algorithmic bias (p=0.030). Despite these concerns, most physicians valued AI in healthcare and academic research and demonstrated strong interest in training and collaboration. Qualitative findings showed optimism and frequent use of AI tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, often described as “Google replacements.” However, physicians also highlighted ethical issues and the need for local training and infrastructure improvement. Conclusion: Physicians generally welcome the use of AI in healthcare and research but emphasize the necessity of ethical guidelines, peer collaboration, and formal education. To ensure responsible adoption, addressing infrastructural and trust barriers will be essential for guaranteeing that AI technologies improve rather than undermine patient care and research integrity.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.

documents.abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous flying cars relies heavily on artificial intelligence, making public trust in AI a prerequisite for willingness to fly. However, how AI-related attributes shape this trust and adoption willingness remains underexplored. Based on the integrative model of trust, this study investigates how negative AI attitudes and AI literacy shape public willingness to adopt autonomous flying cars, with trust playing a key mediating role and AI self-efficacy acting as a moderator. Based on survey data collected from 420 respondents, mediation analysis demonstrates that trust plays a predominant mediating role in the relationship between AI attitudes and willingness to fly. AI literacy is examined along various dimensions, such as technical understanding and critical appraisal, which yield divergent effects on trust. While technical understanding is positively associated with trust, critical appraisal shows no significant effect. This suggests that in early-stage adoption, trust is driven more by prior knowledge than by cognitive evaluation. Moreover, an Artificial Neural Network coupled with explainable machine learning is further employed for nonlinear insights, revealing significant nonlinear relationships between these factors and willingness to fly, particularly the opposing effects of critical appraisal. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for UAM policymaking and sustainable urban mobility.

documents.abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.

documents.abstract: Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing human authority, containment, intervention, and oversight in advanced AI agents. Version 1.5 builds on v1.4 and adds source-qualified analysis of unintended actions against real external systems, a supplementary Philadelphia false-tip review, and separate discovery, containment, and notification intervals. It examines monitoring evaluations, independent-control proposals, implementation vulnerability disclosures, governance responses, and prospective risk assessments. An evidence-disposition appendix accounts for the daily safety review topics while preserving source-access limits and uncorroborated leads. The original five pilot cases, six dimensions, qualitative severity definitions, and prior corrections are retained. HIC-006 is supplementary and its severity remains unresolved. Proposed tests are not completed studies. This is an unreviewed conceptual working paper without completed independent human coding or empirical validation. AI tools assisted source retrieval, editorial comparison, drafting, and document preparation; this revision is not private-log verification, independent reproduction, or peer review. Previous releases remain preserved under the same concept DOI.

documents.abstract: Visually impaired people face obstacles in accessing activities that depend heavily on vision and may involve physical constraints. Although assistive technologies are available, they rarely address the needs of people with residual vision who wish to exploit their visual abilities. Virtual reality (VR) offers opportunities in this direction. This paper presents an immersive VR system designed to provide museum experiences for visually impaired users. Developed in collaboration with domain experts, the system combines a virtual environment with interaction techniques. Gesture recognition and voice commands support spatial awareness and object interaction, while enhanced visualizations highlight details that are difficult to perceive. To verify the suitability of the proposed method, an exploratory usability study involving 14 participants with severe low vision was carried out. The evaluation combined the System Usability Scale (SUS) and a post-experience interview, showing well perceived usability, engagement, and positive user acceptance.

documents.abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents.

documents.abstract: Critical thinking is a core competence in teacher education, essential for navigating complex classroom realities and making informed pedagogical decisions. This study explores the potential of simulation as a pedagogical method to enhance critical thinking among pre-service teachers and thereby support the development of professional suitability. Employing a mixed-methods design, the research combines survey data collected before and after a simulation intervention (N = 114) with qualitative insights from focus-group discussions. The findings suggest that simulation fosters deeper cognitive engagement by enabling iterative reflection, perspective-taking, and critical dialogue within realistic educational scenarios. Participants described a dynamic reflective cycle of thinking, speaking, acting, and rethinking that enhanced their ability to assess multiple viewpoints and question assumptions. Survey responses revealed a significant shift in the perceived value of simulation for developing critical thinking. Notably, the study also found that the pre-service teachers initially held a relatively narrow understanding of critical thinking prior to the intervention. This study contributes to the growing body of research on practice-based teacher education by examining how simulation can be purposefully integrated to support the development of critical thinking in a structured and sustainable manner.
